title: Taylor orders and logarithmic differential transforms
statement:
Let $N\hookrightarrow Z$ be a smooth closed pair of finite-type $\mathbf Q$-schemes and let $E$ be a finite ordered simple normal crossings boundary transverse to $N$ (its local equations restrict to distinct coordinate parameters on $N$). Let $I\subset\mathcal O_N$ be coherent and $d\ge1$. Write $\operatorname{ord}_x I=\sup\{q\ge0:I_x\subseteq\mathfrak m_x^q\}$, with value $\infty$ for zero, and $\operatorname{cosupp}(I,d)=\{x:\operatorname{ord}_xI\ge d\}$. A test transformation is an open restriction, a smooth-center blowup in cosupport with normal crossings with $E$, a product with a line adjoining its zero section to $E$, or a blowup of the intersection of two boundary hypersurfaces. For a cosupport blowup use the strict transform of $N$ and the ideal $e^{-d}\sigma^*I$, where $e$ is the exceptional equation; for the last two operations use ordinary pullback. Let $D_E^jI$ be the coherent ideal generated by derivatives of sections of $I$ of length at most $j$ using $\mathbf Q$-derivations preserving every boundary ideal, and put $D^j=D_\varnothing^j$. In characteristic zero the Taylor criterion gives
$$\operatorname{ord}_xI\ge q\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (D^{q-1}I)_x\subseteq\mathfrak m_x\quad(q\ge1).$$
The order function is upper semicontinuous; if $I$ is nonzero on every component it is locally bounded and has finite image on quasi-compact $N$. For coherent ideals $I,J$ at a point of a smooth scheme, $\operatorname{ord}_x(IJ)=\operatorname{ord}_xI+\operatorname{ord}_xJ$ and $\operatorname{ord}_x(I+J)=\min(\operatorname{ord}_xI,\operatorname{ord}_xJ)$, with the usual infinite-value conventions. Orders and $D_E^j$ commute with smooth pullback. For $0\le j<d$ and any finite test sequence, the transform with mark $d-j$ satisfies
$$(D_E^jI)_t\subseteq D_{E_t}^j(I_t).$$
If $E=\varnothing$ and $\operatorname{ord}_x I=d$, then locally one can choose $f\in I$ and a coordinate direction $v$ such that $\partial_v^d f$ is a unit and $h=\partial_v^{d-1}f$ cuts out a smooth hypersurface. If more generally $h\in D_E^{d-1}I$ has order one and $V(h)$ is transverse to $E$, its mark-one transforms $h_t$ have order one and $V(h_t)$ is transverse to $E_t$ near the transformed cosupport; also $h_t\in D_{E_t}^{d-1}I_t$ and $\operatorname{cosupp}(I_t,d)\subseteq V(h_t)$. These assertions are local near cosupport, so charts where it is empty may be discarded. proof.text: Fix a point $x$ and put $R=\mathcal O_{N,x}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x$, $K=\kappa(x)$. Smoothness gives a Noetherian regular local ring. Choose regular parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_r$. They form a regular sequence, so the cited graded-polynomial theorem identifies $\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m}R$ with $K[T_1,\ldots,T_r]$, sending $T_i$ to the initial class of $t_i$. This identification will be used for orders and leading forms, including when $r=0$.

source.place: Stacks algebra.tex Tags 00NQ (lemma-regular-ring-CM), 00LN (lemma-regular-quasi-regular), and 061P/061N for the canonical graded-polynomial map; Tag 00NO (lemma-regular-graded) is its regular-local consequence.

proof.text: The residue field $K/\mathbf Q$ is finitely generated and separable by the two cited field lemmas. Hence $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\to\Omega_{R/\mathbf Q}\otimes_R K$ is injective. The differential module is finite free at $x$. Extend the independent vectors $dt_i$ to a basis of its residue vector space, take the dual functionals on that vector space, and lift their coefficients in a free module basis to $R$. The universal property of differentials gives actual $\mathbf Q$-derivations $\delta_i:R\to R$ with $\delta_i(t_j)\equiv\delta_{ij}\pmod {\mathfrak m}$. These derivations extend to a neighbourhood: write them in a local finite differential frame and shrink to clear the finitely many denominators. No rationality or closedness assumption on $x$ was used.

source.place: Stacks algebra.tex Tag 00TU (lemma-computation-differential), morphisms.tex Tag 02G1 (lemma-smooth-omega-finite-locally-free), and Tag 00RO (lemma-universal-omega).

proof.text: Every derivation sends $\mathfrak m^a$ into $\mathfrak m^{a-1}$ for $a\ge1$, by Leibniz on products. Thus $I_x\subseteq\mathfrak m^q$ implies $(D^{q-1}I)_x\subseteq\mathfrak m$. Conversely choose $f\in I_x$ outside $\mathfrak m^q$. Among $0\le a<q$ there is a largest $s$ with $f\in\mathfrak m^s$, so $f\notin\mathfrak m^{s+1}$; no finiteness-of-order theorem is needed here. By Step 1 write $f=\sum_{|\beta|=s}\widetilde c_\beta t^\beta+r$, where $r\in\mathfrak m^{s+1}$ and some $c_\alpha\ne0$ in $K$. Apply the fixed ordered composite $\delta_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\delta_r^{\alpha_r}$ of Step 2; no commutation of these derivations is assumed. Its value modulo $\mathfrak m$ is $\alpha!c_\alpha$: the remainder stays in $\mathfrak m$, and the only surviving Leibniz terms differentiate each parameter factor exactly once. Differentiating a coefficient, or a factor already differentiated, leaves an undifferentiated parameter. The factorial is nonzero in characteristic zero. The resulting unit is in $D^{q-1}I$, proving the converse. For $s=0$ use $f$ itself.

source.place: BM §3.2, Lemma 3.2(3); explicit leading-form argument using Steps 1--2.

proof.text: By the derivative lemma, $D^{q-1}I$ is coherent. On an affine neighbourhood choose finitely many generators $a_i$; the Taylor criterion identifies $\{x:\operatorname{ord}_x I\ge q\}$ there with $V(a_1,\ldots,a_l)$, so it is closed. This proves upper semicontinuity, with the value $\infty$ allowed. If $I$ is nonzero on every component then $I_x\ne0$ for every $x$: a zero stalk would, by finite generation, give a neighbourhood on which $I=0$, containing a generic point of a component through $x$. Here $R$ is Noetherian local, $\mathfrak m$ is its Jacobson radical and $M=R$ is generated by $1$. Thus the cited Krull intersection theorem with ideal $\mathfrak m$ shows that a nonzero germ has finite order, hence $I_x$ has finite order $a$. The open set $\{\operatorname{ord} I<a+1\}$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ with an upper bound. A finite subcover of these neighbourhoods bounds the orders on any quasi-compact $N$, giving a finite image. The zero ideal has order $\infty$ everywhere, so the nonzero-component hypothesis is essential.

source.place: BM §3.2 for coherent derivative ideals; Stacks algebra.tex Tag 00IQ (lemma-intersection-powers-ideal-module), part (2), applied with the maximal ideal; elementary closed-zero-locus and compactness argument.

proof.text: At a fixed point, the order of a finitely generated ideal is the minimum of the orders of its generators. For nonzero $I_x,J_x$ let these minima be $a,b$ and choose $f,g$ attaining them. Their initial forms in the graded polynomial domain of Step 1 are nonzero, and their product is nonzero of degree $a+b$. Thus $fg\notin\mathfrak m^{a+b+1}$, while every generator product lies in $\mathfrak m^{a+b}$. This gives $\operatorname{ord}_x(IJ)=a+b$. If either ideal is zero, the product is zero and the infinite-value formula follows. Finally $(I+J)_x\subseteq\mathfrak m^q$ if and only if both $I_x,J_x\subseteq\mathfrak m^q$, proving the minimum formula, including unit and zero ideals.

source.place: Stacks algebra.tex Tag 00NO, lemma-regular-graded; direct calculation with initial forms from Step 1.

proof.text: Let $y\mapsto x$ under a smooth pullback and set $A=\mathcal O_{N,x}$, $B=\mathcal O_{N_Y,y}$. The smooth affine/ring comparison gives an essentially smooth local map; both rings are essentially of finite type over $\mathbf Q$. Apply the smooth tangent-cone extension theorem. The induced map $\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m}A\to\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak n}B$ is the inclusion into the scalar extension followed by a polynomial extension, so it is injective. Thus each nonzero germ from $A$ keeps its finite order in $B$. If $I_x=0$, its extension is zero, and both orders are infinite. Otherwise let $a$ be the minimum order of finitely many generators of $I_x$. All their images lie in $\mathfrak n^a$, so every $B$-linear combination does too; an image attaining $a$ remains outside $\mathfrak n^{a+1}$ by graded injectivity. Hence $\operatorname{ord}_y(I\mathcal O_{N_Y})=\operatorname{ord}_x I$, also for a unit ideal. The derivative lemma gives exactly $D_{E_Y}^j(I\mathcal O_{N_Y})=(D_E^jI)\mathcal O_{N_Y}$ for each $j$. Its smooth-pullback clause includes relative derivations and split boundary components, so no equality of residue fields or relative-dimension restriction is imposed.

source.place: BM Lemma 3.2(4); ILO VIII 2.3.13 and the cited smooth local tangent-cone extension theorem for orders.

proof.text: Fix $0\le j<d$ and a finite test word. Prove by induction on its length that the transform $A_r$ of $(D_E^jI,d-j)$ is defined and $A_r\subseteq D_{E_r}^jI_r$. At length zero this is equality. At stage $r$, derivative order loss from the single-transform lemma gives $\operatorname{cosupp}(I_r,d)\subseteq\operatorname{cosupp}(D_{E_r}^jI_r,d-j)\subseteq\operatorname{cosupp}(A_r,d-j)$. Hence a chosen cosupport center for $I_r$ is allowed for both derivative ideals. Apply the single-transform inclusion to $(I_r,d)$, obtaining $(D_{E_r}^jI_r)'\subseteq D_{E_{r+1}}^jI_{r+1}$. Pullback preserves ideal inclusion. For a controlled blowup, the chart theorem makes $N_{r+1}$ smooth and $e$ an exceptional coordinate. Its nonempty local rings are regular by the smooth-over-a-field regularity theorem, hence domains by the regular-local-domain lemma, and the coordinate $e$ is nonzero in each of them, so multiplication by $e^{d-j}$ is injective. Both ideals are coherent by induction. Apply the chart theorem separately with mark $d-j$ to $A_r$ and $D_{E_r}^jI_r$, using the center containments just proved: both controlled transforms are regular. Their inclusion before division therefore implies inclusion after division by $e^{d-j}$. Therefore $A_{r+1}\subseteq(D_{E_r}^jI_r)'\subseteq D_{E_{r+1}}^jI_{r+1}$. Open restrictions, line products and exceptional-intersection tests use ordinary pullback in this induction. If a blowup fits two descriptions, keep its chosen transform convention fixed. This proves the finite-word assertion, also for empty strict transforms.

source.place: BM Corollaries 3.4--3.6, pp.622--623; explicit induction on the test sequence.

proof.text: Suppose $E=\varnothing$ and $\operatorname{ord}_x I=d$. Some local generator $f$ has order $d$. Choose an etale coordinate chart on $N$ using the smooth local normal form. Use the cited centered Taylor map $\tau_x:\mathcal O_{N,x}\to\kappa(x)[[W_1,\ldots,W_n]]$, defined by completion at the rational point after residue-field extension. The degree-$d$ homogeneous term $P$ of $\tau_x(f)$ is nonzero: by Step 3 an iterated derivative of length $d$ is nonzero, and every derivation is a linear combination of coordinate derivations. The latter assertion follows from the polynomial differential basis and formally etale differential base change. Derivatives of shorter length vanish, so variable coefficients do not affect that conclusion. Choose $v\in\mathbf Q^n$ with $P(v)\ne0$. Such a vector exists because a nonzero polynomial over any extension of the infinite field $\mathbf Q$ cannot vanish on all $\mathbf Q^n$, by induction on the number of variables and the one-variable root bound. After an invertible rational linear coordinate change, $v$ is a coordinate direction. The Taylor coefficient formula gives $\partial_v^d f(x)=d!P(v)\ne0$. Shrink so this derivative is a unit. Then $h=\partial_v^{d-1}f$ vanishes at $x$ and $\partial_vh$ is a unit. Replacing that coordinate by $h$ gives an etale chart by the differential criterion, so $V(h)$ is smooth near $x$. For $d=1$ take $h=f$; if $\dim_x N=0$ no positive finite ideal order occurs.

source.place: BM Exercise 4.4(2), p.625, extended from a principal ideal by choosing a minimal-order generator; Stacks Tags 054L, 00RX and 02GU for coordinate inputs.

proof.text: Now start with a local section $h\in D_E^{d-1}I$ of order one and transverse to $E$, shrinking around its zero locus as in the assertion. The order-loss bound gives $D_E^{d-1}I\subseteq\mathfrak m_x$ at every $x$ in cosupport, so $h$ vanishes there. Apply Step 7 with $j=d-1$. The transform of the subideal $(h)$ with mark one stays inside the transform of $D_E^{d-1}I$, since both divide by $e$ in a controlled blowup and use ordinary pullback otherwise. Thus, whenever the hypersurface transform is defined, $h_r\in D_{E_r}^{d-1}I_r$, and derivative order loss implies $\operatorname{cosupp}(I_r,d)\subseteq V(h_r)$. In particular each subsequent cosupport center is contained scheme-theoretically in $V(h_r)$: the local rings of the smooth center are regular and hence domains. At the generic point of each local component its residue field is its fraction field; vanishing there forces the restricted germ to be zero, since a domain injects into its fraction field. This supplies the hypothesis for the coordinate argument in the next two steps.

source.place: BM Corollary 4.1, pp.624--625; order loss and Corollary 3.5; Stacks Tag 00NP (lemma-regular-domain) for the reduced-center argument.

proof.text: For a cosupport-center blowup, work at a point of the smooth center $C\subseteq V(h_r)$ and choose its normal-crossing coordinates with the old boundary. Transversality of $V(h_r)$ means that $dh_r$ is independent of the boundary differentials. Write $h_r=\sum a_i u_i$ in the coordinate generators of $\mathcal I_{C,N_r}$. Some coefficient of a nonboundary center generator is a unit; otherwise $dh_r$ would be a combination of the boundary differentials at this point. Replace that generator by $h_r$. The ideals of $C$ are unchanged (solve for the replaced generator using its unit coefficient), all boundary coordinates are unchanged, and the Jacobian criterion makes this an etale coordinate change. The controlled blowup chart theorem applies since the center is smooth, is in cosupport, and has normal crossings. In the chart with pivot $h_r$, the mark-one transform is $h_r/h_r=1$, so Step 9 makes the transformed cosupport empty there. Every other pivot chart has $h_{r+1}=h_r/e$ as a nonboundary coordinate, independent of $e$ and the strict-transform boundary coordinates. Consequently its zero set is smooth and transverse to the full new boundary. This also proves regularity of the mark-one transform. Components swallowed by the center have empty strict transform and impose no assertion.

source.place: BM §3.1, Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 4.1; Stacks Tag 02GU for the coordinate replacement, and the cited controlled chart theorem.

proof.text: For an exceptional-intersection blowup use boundary coordinates $x_1,x_2$, with $h_r$ an additional independent coordinate; complete these to etale coordinates by the differential criterion. This is possible because $V(h_r)$ is transverse to every boundary stratum. In the $x_1$ chart the new coordinates are $e=x_1$, $u=x_2/x_1$, $h_r$ and the unchanged coordinates, with boundary $e=0$, $u=0$ and the remaining old boundary equations. The $x_2$ chart is identical with the indices exchanged. Here the mark-one convention is ordinary pullback: $h_{r+1}=h_r$, still an independent coordinate, so its zero set remains smooth and transverse. These are precisely the coordinate blowup charts of the cited permissible-chart theorem; its regular-ring hypothesis follows from smoothness, and the center indices are the two boundary indices. For a line product, adjoining its coordinate $t$ puts $h_r$ and $t$ in distinct coordinate positions; the new boundary includes $t=0$. Ordinary pullback again preserves the claimed properties. Open restriction preserves the same charts.

source.place: BM Definitions 2.4--2.5, §3.1 and Corollary 4.1; ILO VIII Lemma 4.2.9 coordinate charts, printed p.121.

proof.text: Induct simultaneously along the test word. Initially $h_0=h$ has order one along its zero set and is transverse to $E$. Step 9 makes each cosupport center permissible for $(h_r,1)$. Steps 10--11 give the next regular mark-one transform and its smooth transverse zero set; Step 9 then gives membership in $D_{E_{r+1}}^{d-1}I_{r+1}$ and containment of the next cosupport. At a point of that cosupport the transformed equation vanishes and is a coordinate, hence has order exactly one. The pivot charts with equation $1$, or any other charts with empty cosupport, can be discarded. Thus all persistence assertions hold locally near transformed cosupport for every finite word. No claim is made that $h_r$ vanishes at points outside that locus.

source.place: BM Corollary 4.1; simultaneous induction using Steps 7 and 9--11.
